title: Symmetric Tree
description: Brute force to optimized: inverting a copy then comparing versus a direct mirrored recursive comparison.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given the root of a binary tree, check whether it is a mirror of itself (symmetric around its center).

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","root of a binary tree"],["Output","true if the tree is symmetric around its center, false otherwise"],["Goal","Recursively compare the left and right subtrees in MIRRORED order"],["Constraints","Up to 1000 nodes"]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Mirror image of itself\"","A recursive comparison of two subtrees where the recursive calls swap which sides are compared (outer with outer, inner with inner)"]]}

blocks.text: A tree is symmetric exactly when its left subtree is the MIRROR IMAGE of its right subtree: the two roots' values must match, the LEFT subtree's left child must mirror the RIGHT subtree's right child, and the LEFT subtree's right child must mirror the RIGHT subtree's left child, recursively.

blocks.title: Analogy: Checking If a Face Is Symmetric Using a Mirror Line
blocks.text: Picture checking if a face is symmetric by comparing its left half against its right half, feature by feature, but reading the right half backward (mirrored) so that corresponding features (like both eyes) are compared to each other correctly.

blocks.caption: Compare left and right subtrees in mirrored order: outer with outer, inner with inner

blocks.text: Symmetric = true. The two 2s match, then (3,4) under the left 2 mirrors (4,3) under the right 2.
Symmetric = false. The 3s are both on the inside (right of left 2, right of right 2), breaking the mirror.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A tree is symmetric exactly when its left subtree mirrors its right subtree.

Observation 2: "A mirrors B" means: both are empty (trivially true), or both are non-empty with equal values, AND A's left mirrors B's right, AND A's right mirrors B's left, recursively.

Observation 3: This recursive mirror-check, applied to the root's two children, directly answers the overall symmetry question, without ever constructing an explicit inverted copy of either subtree.
This leads to a direct recursive mirror-comparison function, comparing outer children with outer children and inner children with inner children at every level.
Conceptually, invert one subtree entirely (as a separate copy), then compare it against the other subtree directly for structural and value equality.
Why the code is written this way

items: Building an explicit inverted copy before comparing implements the mirror concept literally.
This wastes O(n) extra space constructing a whole copy that is immediately discarded; a direct mirrored comparison needs no such copy.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n) to invert plus O(n) to compare.
Space: O(n) for the inverted copy.
Limitation: comparing left and right subtrees directly in mirrored order, without constructing any copy, achieves the same result using only recursion stack space.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Define isMirror(a, b): if both are null, return true. If exactly one is null, return false. Otherwise, return true only if a.val equals b.val, AND isMirror(a.left, b.right) is true, AND isMirror(a.right, b.left) is true (note the swapped sides). The overall answer is true for an empty tree, or isMirror(root.left, root.right) otherwise.
Compare the left and right subtrees directly, recursively, always pairing OUTER children together and INNER children together, with no separate inversion step.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Call","Result"],"rows":[["isMirror(2(left), 2(right))","values match, continue"],["isMirror(3, 3) (left.left vs right.right)","true"],["isMirror(4, 4) (left.right vs right.left)","true"],["Overall","true, symmetric"]]}

blocks.text: Deliberately swapping which children get compared against each other (a's left against b's right, a's right against b's left) exactly captures the mirror relationship at every level of recursion, without ever needing to physically construct an inverted copy of either subtree; the recursion naturally handles arbitrarily deep mirrored structures.

blocks.text: Symmetric Tree is a clean example of comparing two structures with a deliberately swapped recursive pairing, avoiding any need to build an explicit mirrored copy.

items: Comparing a.left with b.left and a.right with b.right (same-side pairing) instead of the mirrored (opposite-side) pairing this problem actually requires.
Forgetting the base cases for one or both sides being null.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["Empty tree","Considered symmetric (trivially true)."],["Single node tree","Considered symmetric (no children to compare)."]]}

blocks.text: Explicitly stating "compare outer children together and inner children together" clarifies the mirrored pairing precisely, avoiding a same-side comparison mistake.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "check if a tree is a mirror image of itself", think: recursively compare subtrees with swapped (mirrored) child pairing.

items: How would you solve this iteratively using a queue, pushing pairs of nodes to compare?
Invert Binary Tree, which uses the same mirroring concept but transforms the tree instead of comparing it.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Both approaches cost O(n) time; the direct mirrored comparison avoids the brute force's O(n) extra space for an inverted copy.

items: Pattern: recursive comparison of two structures using a deliberately swapped (mirrored) pairing.
Core Idea: a.left mirrors b.right and a.right mirrors b.left, recursively, starting from root.left and root.right.
Space: O(n) for the brute force's copy, O(h) recursion depth for the direct approach.
Most Important Observation: mirrored pairing (outer with outer, inner with inner) avoids needing an explicit inverted copy.
Interview Difficulty: a classic, easy recursive tree comparison problem.
One line memory trick: compare crossed, not straight.
